headline: The dispatch offered two forks and production is in neither. The upstream export CAPABILITY exists and is live, a CREDENTIAL exists and carries paid entitlement, and the CLIENT CONTRACT the smartsite-mcp proxy is coded against has never existed in any server. POST /tools/export_instrument 404s on hauska-mcp-server and appears in exactly two places in the whole estate: the caller that calls it, and a test that mocks it. Configuring the two env vars would therefore not have fixed the tool; it would have converted an honest not-configured refusal into a 404 HTML body on a tool that then reported itself configured. Item 2 was not taken. Item 3 was, and the tool now refuses honestly to every tier and is advertised as not ready.

leave_behind.note: The capability and the credential both exist and were proven live in this close. Three rulings gate the build: (1) there is no upstream 'brief' export kind, so either brief is dropped from the kind enum or it is served from cortex instead; (2) upstream is two-hop refresh-then-download with per-format enums, so the one-shot client signature must change or the server must orchestrate both hops; (3) the upstream tools are public-paid and SDK-metered per refresh while smartsite-mcp callers already pay Stripe, so wiring them without a ruling double-charges. Also required: mount HAUSKA_MCP_KEY as a secretKeyRef in .github/workflows/cloud-run-deploy-smartsite-mcp.yml, never a literal and never a manual services update, and never bind the base URL to PRODUCTION_HAUSKA_MCP_URL, which is a Postgres DSN.

LESSON: A starved control can be starved of a precondition that COULD NEVER HAVE BEEN SUPPLIED. Before configuring a missing env var, probe the endpoint that var points at. P-109's two variables were absent, and supplying them would have produced a 404 while making the tool report itself configured. Absent config is not automatically a config bug.

A client-side path constant is a claim about a server. POST /tools/export_instrument existed in exactly two places in the whole estate: the caller, and a test that mocked the caller. The mock was the only thing making the contract look real. When a test fixture is the sole corroboration of an integration, the integration is unverified.

An anti-vacuity guard must assert the INSTRUMENT is intact, never that the DEFECT is present. The first version of this lane's control asserted that tools.ts still contains a hardcoded refusal; fixing the defect broke the guard. Pin the defect text as a fixture constant instead.

TypeScript's narrowing over a readonly catalog array is a real control. Flipping a tool to readiness 'blocked' in the catalog forces removal of its handler case (TS2678), and removing a live tool's handler forces TS7030. Where a type can express the constraint, it needs no test and cannot be forgotten - but it could NOT catch the P-109 defect itself, because a live tool refusing at runtime type-checks perfectly.
A secret's NAME is not its type. PRODUCTION_HAUSKA_MCP_URL and STAGING_HAUSKA_MCP_URL in hauska-prod-497015 are Postgres DSNs, not HTTP base URLs. Read a secret before binding it to anything.
DEAD-END: Do not try to reach Hauska's export capability over REST. hauska-mcp-server registers no /tools/* route of any kind; it is MCP JSON-RPC on POST /mcp plus /health, /llms.txt, /admin, /metering/summary, /auth/whoami, /gate-probe. The only REST-shaped tool call is POST /admin/introspection/tools/:name/call, which is admin-auth'd and is not a product path.

Do not delete export_instrument from SMARTSITE_MCP_TOOLS to stop advertising it. SmartsiteToolName is derived from that array, so the name's removal breaks case labels in inputSchemaFor too and cascades into the ring-fenced tools.ts. readiness 'blocked' achieves the catalog and runtime halves with one entry edit plus one forced case removal.

Do not run `npx tsc ... | tail -20; echo $?` and read that as the typecheck result. It reports the pipe's exit code. This lane briefly recorded TSC_EXIT=0 for a run that had actually failed with TS2678.

adversarialReview.strongestObjection: This lane turned a working-looking tool off. If someone later supplies the env vars expecting a fix, they will find the tool blocked and may read the block as the bug.
adversarialReview.answer: The tool was never working; it returned not_ready on every call in production and the deployed README already said so. The block is now readable from three places that all name P-109 item 3 and the measured 404: the blockedReason returned to the caller, the llms.txt line, and a comment at the old handler site listing the rewire target tools. Supplying the env vars now changes nothing, which is the point - and a test asserts exactly that, including that no fetch is attempted.
adversarialReview.secondObjection: The item-4 control is text matching over source, and this operation's own memory says text search cannot answer structural questions.
adversarialReview.answer: Correct, and that is why the structural half is carried by the compiler, which is named and not claimed as this lane's work. The text predicates cover the one thing the compiler cannot see - a live tool with a runtime refusal - and both are wrapped in anti-vacuity guards that were shown firing on a rename in each direction. The close states in the test file and here that these are internal-consistency checks, that one party can satisfy both sides, and that the meaning-shaped version is unbuilt.
adversarialReview.thirdObjection: CP1 declared zero tools.ts edits and the lane made one anyway.
adversarialReview.answer: Recorded as a failed pre-registered prediction with its falsifier and the verbatim compiler error, in CP2, rather than quietly widened. The edit is one contiguous region at line 846, in a file whose only open-PR hunks are at 88, 373 and 533.
